The high water mark of the western genre ended quite a while before video games became mainstream, I guess.

What's the last big-budget movie blockbuster Western you can think of? That True Grit remake is the one that comes to mind for me. Cowboys Vs. Aliens maybe, but that's kind of stretching both 'Western' and 'blockbuster'. Django Unchained was a frontier setting, but I wouldn't really call it a Western in the traditional sense. And I can't think of any popular Western TV shows at all.

Compare that to how many zombie movies you can think of. The popularity is waning now, but good god, for a while there they were everywhere. People watched The Walking Dead religiously. Books, TV, movies - roundabout 2010, zombies were one of the primary fixtures of the zeitgeist - and lo and behold, there were tons of zombie games, as well.

Games are generally going to follow whatever themes and settings are currently capturing the public's imagination. The golden age of Westerns was really prior to video games. You had a lot of frontier-themed games in the 80's, because programmers were postwar Boomers feeding their own childhood nostalgia, just like 30-somethings do now with the 90's, but the American infatuation with cowboys has subsided a lot in the intervening years - even in Country music, it's exceedingly rare to see a Blake Shelton or a Carrie Underwood in a cowboy hat.

I think it's mostly just the unending wax and wane of public interest. Westerns aren't 'it' right now, and that means you're not going to see many developers investing resources in making those kinds of games.

I expect with both the new Fallout and Mad Max we'll be seeing an upswing of post-apocalyptica in the near future, though.

I think that the problem is that westerns are a very stripped down genre, that is limited technology juxtaposed to the loneliness of expansive wastelands. Westerns don't seem to be about straight up action but rather the gaps around the action that provide the framework of the action. And this just doesn't really translate that well in terms of game mechanics with regard to pacing due to games by necessity being the antithesis of this, I.E., non-stop action for instant gratification. For example if you think about all your classic westerns then they normally revolve around long drawn out stretches of seeing the bad guys assemble at a train station waiting for the hero for a resulting confrontation. In a cinematic context this works due to the gradual build up of tension but for a game - not so much.
